content.description: Ludwig van Beethoven, from Bonn to Vienna, composes his greatest works as he goes deaf and invents the romantic genius.

hero.hook: Deaf, he composed the anthem of joy for all of humanity.

blocks.text: **Ludwig van Beethoven** (**1770**-**1827**) is the model of the modern genius: wild hair, iron will, a fight against fate. Beyond the myth, his life marks a break. The composer is no longer a court servant but a sovereign creator.
He turned entertainment music into a philosophical language. And he designed his largest sound structures, the Ninth Symphony among them, in almost total silence.

Born in [[Bonn]] in **1770**, Ludwig grew up under a brutal father, **Johann**, who wanted to turn him into the next [[Mozart]]. Rehearsals late into the night forged an early technique, and a will of iron.

blocks.caption: The young Beethoven in Bonn: a childhood under pressure

blocks.text: In **1792**, he moved to [[Vienna]], the musical capital. He studied briefly with **Joseph Haydn**. A piano virtuoso and a stunning improviser, he refused to fawn on his patrons: he meant to be the equal of princes. His early style, still classical, already announced violent contrasts and larger forms.
He was so careless about his appearance in his Vienna years that friends sometimes swapped his worn clothes for new ones while he slept, and he never noticed.

sections.title: From Bonn to Vienna: the equal of princes

blocks.text: Between **1798** and **1801**, tinnitus and hearing loss set in. For a star pianist, it was a catastrophe. In **1802**, in the village of **Heiligenstadt**, he wrote the **Heiligenstadt Testament**, a letter to his brothers that he never sent. In it he confessed to suicidal thoughts, then chose to live in order to compose everything he carried inside him.

blocks.caption: The Heiligenstadt Testament: despair turning into a decision to create

blocks.text: The [[heroic period]] began. The Third Symphony, known as the *Eroica*, was first dedicated to [[Napoleon Bonaparte]]. When Napoleon crowned himself emperor, Beethoven raged and withdrew the dedication. The work revolutionized the genre through its length and its intensity.
To feel the vibrations better, he had the legs sawn off his pianos so that they sat directly on the floor.

Late in his life, Beethoven was almost completely deaf. In **1824**, he finished the **Ninth Symphony**: for the first time, soloists and a chorus entered a symphony. The finale is built on [[Ode to Joy]], the poem by **Friedrich von Schiller**, turned into a message of brotherhood.

blocks.caption: The Ninth: the human voice enters the symphony

blocks.text: At the premiere, unable to hear the ovation, he kept beating time. The contralto **Caroline Unger** turned him around to see the crowd on its feet. [[Ode to Joy]] later became a European anthem of peace. His last quartets, harsh and modern, would not be understood for decades.
He sometimes clenched a wooden rod between his teeth with the other end on the piano: bone conduction let him “hear” the notes.

sections.title: The Ninth: the Ode to Joy

blocks.text: Beethoven carried music from classicism into [[Romanticism]]: subjectivity, passion, excess. The symphony became a metaphysical drama. [[Brahms]] and [[Mahler]] would live in his shadow. He also opened the way to [[absolute music]], where sound needs nothing outside itself. At his funeral in **1827**, more than **20,000** people followed the procession through Vienna.

\"Absolute\" music vs program music.explanation: The absolute music (Beethoven) expresses pure emotions without external reference. Program music (Berlioz, Liszt) tells a story. This distinction structures the great aesthetic debate of the romantic 19th century.

\"Absolute\" music vs. program music.explanation: Absolute music (Beethoven) expresses pure emotions without external reference. Program music (Berlioz, Liszt) tells a story. This distinction structures the great aesthetic debate of the romantic 19th century.

Bonn.explanation: City in North Germany, capital of the Electorate of Cologne, where Beethoven was born and spent his youth.

Brahms.explanation: German composer (1833-1897) who took more than twenty years to complete his first symphony, crushed by the monumental shadow of Beethoven.

Mahler.explanation: Composer and conductor (1860-1911) who pushed the symphony genre to its expressive and structural limits after Beethoven.

Mozart.explanation: Prodigious Austrian composer (1756-1791) whose immediate successor Beethoven's father wanted his son to become.

Napoleon Bonaparte.explanation: General then Emperor of the French whose initial republican ideals fascinated Beethoven, before his imperial coronation provoked the composer's anger.

Ode to Joy.explanation: The last movement of the 9th Symphony, based on Schiller's poem, became the official anthem of the European Union in 1985. The universalism of its message (brotherhood of humanity) makes it the symbol of the European ideal of unity.

Romanticism.explanation: 19th-century artistic movement emphasizing the expression of feelings, imagination, and subjectivity over classical rigor.

Vienna.explanation: Capital of the Austrian Empire and world center of classical music where Beethoven spent most of his career.

absolute music.explanation: Aesthetic concept designating music that does not depend on any external narrative or visual support, existing for its own sonic structures.

heroic period.explanation: Creative period of Beethoven marked by grandiose works evoking struggle, victory, and resilience in the face of fate.
